newsitem.title: USA: New York utilities to address restructuring.
newsitem.headline: New York utilities to address restructuring.

text.p: Most electric utilities operating in New York will present their restructuring proposals by the October 1 deadline set by the state Public Service Commission.

Energy Association of New York President Howard Shapiro said Friday "it is my understanding all (the companies) are filing," noting that the commission requested proposals from all utilities operating in the state except Niagara Mohawk Power Corp and Long Island Lighting Co.
One filing, from New York State Electric and Gas Corp could come as early as Friday, a spokeswoman said.
Another, from Central Hudson Gas & Electric Corp is said by sources at other companies to consist of a statement as to why the company is not submitting a restructuring proposal.
A Central Hudson spokesman would only say the company "will have no details until the First."
Consolidated Edison Co of New York Inc will file October 1, spokesman Richard Mulleri said.
Orange & Rockland Utilities Inc and Rochester Gas & Electric Corp also said they will file proposals.
Shapiro said the filings will be accompanied by a status report on the negotiations to create an independent system operator for New York's power transmission system.

The ISO, which is part of the proposal put forward by the commission in May, has been the subject of continuing discussions since then between the seven utilities and the New York Power Authority -- the eight members of the New York Power Pool.
Power Pool spokesmen have declined to discuss those talks, as have spokespersons for the eight members.
This week, the Power Authority said the eight are discussing "a single statewide transmission tariff that could, in large measure, eventually supplant the authority's proposed tarrif.
"The Power Authority expects to file its tariff with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission by the end of 1996, before completion of the Power Pool plan," its statement continued.
However, Shapiro pointed out, the ISO plan is supposed to be filed with FERC by year end.

He also said the filings planned by association members shows the suit the group filed last week seeking a review of the commission order requiring the deregulation plans "should not delay the transition" to a competitive utility industry.

But Carol Murphy, executive director of the Independent Power Producers of New York Inc, believes the utilities are "trying to slow this process down as much as they can," adding this could well result in action by the legislature.
The utilities disagree, with ConEd's Mulleri pointing out "By not filing we could have been liable in a shareholder suit" challenging the lack of action on fiduciary grounds.
The suit did question the Public Service Commission's legislative authority to proceed with its proposal.
Shapiro said this could come "when there is a resolution" of issues now being discussed, stating "there will be a need for implementing legislation."
"I don't really think the utilities want legislation," Murphy said, adding she expects action by both houses of the legislature next year.
This year, the Democrat-controlled assembly passed a the Competition Plus plan put forward by its leadership which proposed changes in commission authority.

The Republican-controlled Senate passed two proposals put forward by Republican Governor George Pataki to provide low cost power for economic development and securitize utilities' requirements to buy power from independent producers, thereby lowering the cost of those commitments.
Shapiro pointed out the securitization proposal was "adopted to a significant degree in California," where the legislature did act on utility deregulation this summer.
Legislative action was also called for at an Assembly Energy Committee hearing in June by spokesmen for ConEd and various groups of power users.
"We need to make changes in law," Energy Committee Chairman Paul Tonko told Reuters last week, stating the utility suit "indicates solidly that the PSC lacks legislative authority."
Statuatory changes would "at least limit visits to the court rooom," he said, calling estimates it will take two years to fully litigate the utility suit "conservative."
After the filing, the commission said it would seek an expedited hearing of the case.
This was still being discussed by utility and commission lawyers this week, Shaprio said. -- Jim Brumm 212-859-1710
